Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Georgian leaders may be blaming Russia for the conflict raging in South Ossetia, but former Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev said Thursday "there is no doubt" that Georgia provoked the clash. Mikhail Gorbachev told CNN's Larry King that Russia called extra troops into Georgia to stem violence. Gorbachev told CNN's Larry King that Russia moved additional forces into South Ossetia in response to "devastation" in the South Ossetia city of Tskhinvali. "This was the use of sophisticated weapons against a small town, against a sleeping people. This was a barbaric assault," said Gorbachev, the last president of the former Soviet Union. But Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili, who also appeared on CNN's "Larry King Live" Thursday, said he was "profoundly shocked" that Mikhail Gorbachev would use a television appearance "for basically vindicating lies and deceptions." Last week, Georgia said it launched an operation into South Ossetia after a cease-fire was broken with artillery fire from Russian separatists that killed 10 people including civilians and peacekeepers. It accused Russia, which also has peacekeepers in the region, of backing the separatists. Hours later, the Russian news agency Interfax reported that Russian authorities said 10 Russian peacekeepers had been killed and 30 wounded in an attack by Georgians. "Western television didn't show what happened in Tskhinvali," Gorbachev said. "Only now they're beginning to show some pictures of the destruction. So this looks to me like it was a well-prepared project. And with any outcome, they wanted to put the blame on Russia."  Watch Gorbachev discuss "barbaric assault" » . He called Georgia's claims that Russia is attempting to dismantle its democracy "all lies from beginning to end." In response, Saakashvili expressed disappointment with the sentiments from Gorbachev, who he said he once respected. "This is the man, Mr. Gorbachev, who helped to, you know, bring down KGB kingdom. And he is the one who is, you know, justifying what the KGB people are doing right now in my country," Saakashvili said. "Shame on him. Shame on you, Mr. Gorbachev, for perpetuating the very regime you helped to defeat and you fought against as the head of the Soviet Union." Gorbachev also said the United States is jeopardizing its fragile relationship with Russia by backing Georgia.  Watch Gorbachev discuss U.S.-Russia relations » . "There is a chance for our two countries to develop a new agenda for cooperation so as to promote both U.S. and Russia interests, and the interests of other countries, and the interests of stability, particularly in the hotspots in different continents," said Gorbachev, who won the Nobel Peace Price in 1990.

(CNN) — Georgian leaders may blame Russia for the conflict raging in South Ossetia, but former Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev said Thursday that “there is no doubt” Georgia provoked the clash.

Gorbachev told CNN’s Larry King that Russia deployed additional troops to South Ossetia to stem the violence following the “devastation” in the city of Tskhinvali.

“This was the use of sophisticated weapons against a small town, against a sleeping people. This was a barbaric assault,” said Gorbachev, the last president of the former Soviet Union.

However, Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili, who also appeared Thursday on CNN’s “Larry King Live,” said he was “profoundly shocked” that Gorbachev would use a television appearance “for basically vindicating lies and deceptions.”

Last week, Georgia said it had launched an operation in South Ossetia after a cease-fire was broken by artillery fire from Russian separatists, killing 10 people, including civilians and peacekeepers. Georgia accused Russia, which also has peacekeepers in the region, of supporting the separatists.

Hours later, the Russian news agency Interfax reported that Russian authorities said 10 Russian peacekeepers had been killed and 30 wounded in an attack by Georgian forces.

“Western television didn’t show what happened in Tskhinvali,” Gorbachev said. “Only now they’re beginning to show some pictures of the destruction. So this looks to me like it was a well-prepared project. And with any outcome, they wanted to put the blame on Russia.”

Watch Gorbachev discuss the “barbaric assault” ».

He described Georgia’s claims that Russia was attempting to dismantle its democracy as “all lies from beginning to end.”

In response, Saakashvili expressed disappointment in Gorbachev, whom he said he had once respected.

“This is the man, Mr. Gorbachev, who helped to, you know, bring down KGB kingdom. And he is the one who is, you know, justifying what the KGB people are doing right now in my country,” Saakashvili said.

“Shame on him. Shame on you, Mr. Gorbachev, for perpetuating the very regime you helped to defeat and you fought against as the head of the Soviet Union.”

Gorbachev also said the United States was jeopardizing its fragile relationship with Russia by supporting Georgia.

outputs.L2:
(CNN) — Although Georgia’s leaders have held Russia responsible for the fighting in South Ossetia, former Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev said Thursday that Georgia unquestionably initiated the confrontation.

Speaking with CNN’s Larry King, Gorbachev said Russia deployed additional troops to South Ossetia to curb the bloodshed after the destruction in Tskhinvali. He described the attack as involving advanced weaponry directed at a small city whose residents were asleep, calling it “barbaric.”

Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili, who also appeared Thursday on CNN’s “Larry King Live,” said he was deeply disturbed that Gorbachev had used his television interview to defend what Saakashvili characterized as falsehoods and deception.

Georgia said the previous week that it began military action in South Ossetia after Russian-backed separatists violated a cease-fire with artillery attacks. According to Georgian officials, those attacks killed 10 people, including civilians and peacekeepers. Georgia also accused Russia—which maintains peacekeeping forces in the area—of supporting the separatists.

Several hours later, Russia’s Interfax news agency reported that Russian authorities said Georgian forces had killed 10 Russian peacekeepers and wounded 30 others.

Gorbachev argued that Western television networks initially failed to show what had occurred in Tskhinvali and had only recently begun broadcasting images of the damage. In his view, the events appeared to have been planned in advance so that Russia would be blamed regardless of the result. He also dismissed Georgia’s allegation that Moscow was trying to destroy Georgian democracy, describing the claim as entirely false.

Saakashvili responded by voicing disappointment in Gorbachev, whom he said he had previously respected. He noted that Gorbachev had helped bring down what he called the “KGB kingdom,” yet was now defending the actions of former KGB figures in Georgia. Saakashvili said Gorbachev should be ashamed for supporting the kind of system he had once opposed and helped defeat while leading the Soviet Union.

Gorbachev further warned that U.S. support for Georgia was putting Washington’s already delicate relationship with Moscow at risk.

The former Soviet leader, who received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990, said the United States and Russia still had an opportunity to create a new framework for cooperation. Such an agenda, he said, could advance the interests of both nations, benefit other countries, and promote stability—especially in conflict zones around the world.
outputs.L3:
Former Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev said that Georgia had provoked the conflict in South Ossetia. According to Gorbachev, Russia deployed additional troops only after Georgian forces used sophisticated weapons to attack Tskhinvali, an operation he described as a “barbaric assault.”

Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili strongly rejected this account, accusing Gorbachev of lending credibility to Russian “lies and deceptions.” Georgia maintained that its forces entered South Ossetia only after Russian-backed separatists violated a cease-fire and killed civilians and peacekeepers.

Gorbachev, however, argued that the Georgian attack had been deliberately planned to shift responsibility for the conflict onto Russia. He also dismissed allegations that Moscow’s actions were part of an effort to dismantle Georgia’s democracy.
outputs.L4:
CNN presented sharply conflicting accounts of the 2008 war in South Ossetia through interviews with former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev and Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili on “Larry King Live.” Their remarks reflected the broader international dispute over how the fighting began and whether Russia’s military intervention was a defensive response or an act of aggression against Georgia.

Gorbachev placed responsibility for the conflict on the Georgian government. He described Georgia’s attack on Tskhinvali, the capital of the separatist region of South Ossetia, as a planned and “barbaric assault.” According to his account, Georgian forces caused extensive destruction and civilian suffering, leaving Russia with little choice but to send troops into the region. He therefore portrayed Moscow’s deployment as a necessary response to the devastation rather than the opening move in a wider invasion.

Saakashvili categorically rejected Gorbachev’s version of events, calling his assertions lies. The Georgian president maintained that Russia bore responsibility for the escalation and disputed the claim that Georgia had deliberately launched an unprovoked war. From his perspective, Moscow used the fighting in South Ossetia to justify a major military operation that extended beyond the separatist territory and into Georgia itself.

By setting the two interviews against each other, CNN underscored the central controversy surrounding the conflict: who initiated the hostilities and how Russia’s subsequent actions should be understood. Gorbachev’s defense of the Russian position and Saakashvili’s forceful denial illustrated how deeply the two sides disagreed not only about the causes of the war, but also about the legitimacy of Russia’s intervention and the meaning of the events in Tskhinvali.
outputs.L5:
### CNN Coverage of Georgian–Russian Relations

CNN has frequently reported on the complex relationship between Georgia and Russia, shaped by decades of political tension and regional conflict. Relations deteriorated sharply after the 2008 war, which resulted in Russia recognizing the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia—territories internationally regarded by most countries as part of Georgia.

Georgian leaders continue to support closer ties with the European Union and NATO, while Russia opposes further Western influence in the region. These competing interests have contributed to political debate within Georgia, public demonstrations, and concerns about national security.

International media outlets such as CNN play an important role in explaining how developments between Georgia and Russia affect the wider South Caucasus, European security, trade, and diplomacy.

counterfactuals.prompt: What did Gorbachev and Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili say to Larry King about the Russia–Georgia war? Answer in the style of a CNN news report.
counterfactuals.output:
**Gorbachev, Saakashvili trade sharply different accounts of Georgia war**

**ATLANTA (CNN)** — Former Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev and Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili offered starkly conflicting versions of the 2008 Russia–Georgia war in interviews with CNN’s Larry King.

Gorbachev said Georgia triggered the conflict by launching an assault on the separatist region of South Ossetia, leaving Russia little choice but to respond and protect Russian citizens and peacekeepers. He blamed Saakashvili’s government for what he described as a reckless military operation and suggested Tbilisi would not have acted without expecting Western — particularly American — support. He also warned against portraying Moscow as the sole aggressor or reviving Cold War-style confrontation.

Saakashvili rejected that account, saying Russia had prepared the invasion in advance and used the fighting in South Ossetia as a pretext to move troops deep into Georgian territory. He characterized the war as an attack on Georgia’s sovereignty and young democracy, accused Russian forces and allied separatists of driving ethnic Georgians from their homes, and appealed for firm international pressure on Moscow.

In essence, Gorbachev portrayed Russia’s actions as a forced response to Georgian aggression; Saakashvili portrayed them as a planned Russian invasion aimed at destabilizing and controlling Georgia.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a news article covering Gorbachev’s claim that Georgia launched a “barbaric assault” on Tskhinvali and Saakashvili’s response.
counterfactuals.output:
**Gorbachev Calls Georgian Attack on Tskhinvali ‘Barbaric’; Saakashvili Rejects Criticism**

**MOSCOW/TBILISI —** Former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev accused Georgia of launching a “barbaric assault” on Tskhinvali, the capital of the breakaway region of South Ossetia, and said Russia had been justified in responding militarily.

Gorbachev said Georgian forces had used heavy weapons against the city when they moved to retake the separatist territory in August 2008. He argued that Moscow could not have ignored the attack, particularly because Russian peacekeepers and residents holding Russian passports were in the region.

Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili rejected Gorbachev’s account, saying Georgia had acted after escalating attacks by South Ossetian forces and Russian involvement in the region. Tbilisi has maintained that its military operation followed sustained provocations and a growing Russian troop presence.

Saakashvili also criticized the former Soviet president for endorsing Moscow’s version of events, arguing that Russia’s subsequent advance deep into Georgia went far beyond protecting South Ossetia and amounted to an invasion of a sovereign country.

The competing statements reflected the continuing dispute over responsibility for the five-day war. Georgian forces entered Tskhinvali on Aug. 7-8, 2008, after days of intensifying clashes. Russia responded with a large-scale military operation that drove Georgian troops from South Ossetia and opened fighting on other fronts.

A European Union-backed inquiry later concluded that Georgia’s shelling of Tskhinvali marked the start of full-scale hostilities, while also finding that the conflict followed years of tension, provocations and increasing Russian pressure. The report said Russia’s initial response could be linked to the defense of its peacekeepers, but that much of the wider military campaign extended beyond reasonable defensive action.

After the war, Moscow recognized South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent states. Georgia and most of the international community continue to regard both territories as part of Georgia.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the competing claims made by Gorbachev and Saakashvili during their appearances on CNN’s “Larry King Live” following the outbreak of fighting in Georgia.
counterfactuals.output:
- **Mikhail Gorbachev** argued that Georgia had started the war by launching a large-scale assault on Tskhinvali, the capital of South Ossetia. He portrayed Russia’s intervention as a necessary response to protect Russian citizens and peacekeepers, not as an attempt to conquer Georgia. He also blamed the United States and other Western countries for emboldening President Mikheil Saakashvili by arming and supporting his government, and called for an investigation into how the fighting began.

- **Mikheil Saakashvili** maintained that Russia’s attack was a long-planned invasion of sovereign Georgia. He said Georgian forces had acted only after sustained separatist attacks and the movement of Russian troops through the Roki Tunnel. He accused Moscow of bombing civilians, conducting or enabling ethnic cleansing, occupying Georgian territory, and seeking regime change and control over Georgia’s strategic position and energy routes.

In short, **Gorbachev described Russia as reacting to Georgian aggression**, while **Saakashvili described Georgia as defending itself against premeditated Russian aggression**.
